newsitem.title: USA: Trade chiefs to build momentum for open markets.
newsitem.headline: Trade chiefs to build momentum for open markets.

text.p: Building momentum for opening global markets in key sectors will be a central issue at this week's meeting of trade chiefs from Japan, European Union, Canada and the United States, U.S. officials said Tuesday.

"The idea is can you find some sectors which are really global and of interest to countries at all levels of development to see if there isn't some sort of cooperative effort that can be made," said one U.S. trade official.

The United States hopes the big four trading partners, the so-called Quadrilateral or "Quad," can build on the momentum of the successful agreements to eliminate tariffs on information technology and open telecommunications market up around the world. The Quad -- Canada, United States, European Union and Japan -- ministers meet Wednesday, Thursday and Friday in Toronto.

The technology agreement, which eliminates tariffs on a number of technologies by 2000, was completed at a meeting of World Trade Organisation ministers in Singapore last December after the four major big trading partners agreed to press for the idea earlier in the year.
In February some 68 countries, under the WTO, agreed to open up their telephone services markets and bring free-trade principles to the $600 billion-a-year industry.

"This is the first meeting that they (the Quad ministers) are having since Singapore and the question is how can they pursue the really positive momentum that has emerged since the ITA and basic telecoms to really keep the WTO moving," said a U.S. official who asked not to be identified.

The ministers will be looking at completion of WTO negotiations by the end of the year on opening up financial services markets and on expanding the information technology accord to include more products, the U.S. official said.
"For us, this QUAD is an opportunity for us to push trade expansion in the WTO and beyond," the official said.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky will also meet individually with trade ministers to discuss pressing bilateral issues including automobile trade with Japanese International Trade and Industry Minister Shinji Sato.
A U.S. trade official said Barshefsky will also likely discuss Japan's efforts to deregulate its economy and beef up domestic demand.
U.S. officials have repeatedly said they want Japan to boost domestic demand to spur its economy and not try to export its way out of recession.

She is also expected to discuss some agriculture issues with Japan as she will in bilateral sessions with European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan and Canadian Trade Ministers Art Eggleton, officials said.
